title: Kathy Baxter - The Human in the Loop: Navigating the Realities of AI for Employee Flourishing

segments.text: KATHY BAXTER: Hi, everyone.
Give them a couple of seconds to bring up my slide.
I am principal architect and a VP of our responsible AI
and tech team at Salesforce, part of the Office
of Ethical and Humane Use.
Very happy to be here today to talk about something
with all of you that is really near and dear to my heart.
And that is, how do we think about creating
AI that works for humans, not the other way around?
And so I'd like to challenge all of you
today for the brief 10 minutes that we have together
to think about, how does this work apply to what
you are doing in your role?
I think all of us have a real opportunity
to think about what it means to not just make AI help us be more
efficient, but to actually increase, to encourage,
to enable human flourishing.
So the question that I would like
for us to think about today is, how
can we design a future where AI doesn't just automate our work,
but actively empowers our human potential to flourish?
So what does a successful human-AI collaboration
look like?
You've probably heard the phrase "human-AI collaboration" many,
many times.
Being able to realize the full potential of that collaboration
requires actual design partnerships
that center on human agency and expertise.
Research has shown that when employees
use AI to draft their work, they can experience drops
in their feelings of control, responsibility, and creativity.
However, we also know that AI can really inspire individuals,
help creative workers to develop more complex designs that
benefit from that unique human touch that only we can provide.
So achieving an effective balance
requires intentional strategies that
leverage the best of human and AI abilities coming together.
What I'd like to propose for you today
are three actionable strategies that you, as leaders,
can help ensure AI encourages flourishing-- again,
not just surviving, not just being faster
at what we're all doing.
The first is by optimizing workflow.
I think many of us here today may be at institutions,
whether it's school, work, where you're being encouraged
to use more AI.
AI-ify everything, token max, automate
as much as you possibly can.
But really, effective leaders don't just hand AI to employees
and say, do more faster.
They guide the employees.
They help them understand what does success really look like,
what is it that we are trying to achieve.
And so we want to ensure that the human-AI relationship is
a true collaboration that activates
the best of both AI and human abilities.
So the human steers the strategy and creative direction
while the AI acts as an autopilot,
handling the rote tasks.
So this really preserves employees' creativity
and ownership while still providing a productivity boost,
ensuring that human oversight of AI is meaningful
and not just a rubber stamp.
The second strategy is implementing mindful friction.
"Mindful friction" is a phrase or a design strategy that
I've been advocating for over a decade.
This principle subtly nudges users
to reflect on their choices.
Oftentimes, we think of friction as a negative thing,
as something to be avoided.
Unfortunately, as we have seen, seamless, frictionless AI
interfaces actively encourage cognitive surrender.
To fix this, we need to design systems
with intentional friction by introducing cognitive forcing
functions or staged reveals.
One example of this is the Delphi method.
This is a structured technique from the 1950s that requires
individuals to independently develop their answers before
sharing them with each other as a way of avoiding groupthink.
And so how might we apply this in human-AI collaboration?
In this case, we want the humans and the AI
to develop their answers, to develop content independently
of each other, and then bring it back to each other
for sharing, iterating, and improving with each round.
So not only can this help mitigate the risk
of human cognitive surrender.
It can also reduce AI sycophancy.
So if the human isn't just asking, or isn't just
giving the AI their idea and asking
the AI to validate it or riff on it,
but instead independently develop their own ideas,
you can get more challenged, more complex solutions
by bringing these together.
The third strategy is fostering sociotechnical resilience.
This involves encouraging a culture of proactive maintenance
to sustain high performance.
So you really want to deliberately invest
in and celebrate human craftsmanship.
This is what truly drives innovation.
Simply handing over all of our tasks to AI
is going to get AI slop, homogenization,
but keeping our human touch in the innovation
is what will truly help all of our organizations succeed.
So institute human-centric lists for meaningful tasks.
This means ensuring that there are some tasks that require
the humans to be involved in.
This isn't just human-in-the-loop where humans
come in after the fact and touch it, validate it,
rubber stamp it.
This means humans at the helm.
We want to ensure that time saved by AI
is used to deepen our own learning, our own development
of our crafts, and strengthen every employee's
unique expertise.
So my goal here is that I hope everyone walks away
identifying AI as a force multiplier
to amplify human craftsmanship.
Many of you may be familiar with the concept
of negative alignment.
This is largely driven the field of ethical AI.
This involves preventing models from causing harms.
And this, of course, is incredibly important,
but it's not sufficient for human flourishing.
Instead, positive alignment is also needed.
It demands that we must design systems
to actively foster human virtue, designing
for wisdom and well-being.
By structuring workflows to protect human agency,
designing with mindful friction, and fostering a culture that
respects human craftsmanship as key to innovation,
leaders can ensure that AI amplifies employees' skills
and well-being.
Instead of outsourcing thinking to AI,
we should design AI to scaffold human learning and empower
people through positive alignment and meta-autonomy.
Thank you.
